Level 3 Curriculum Overview
Level 3 (Expansion) is a 40-lesson course for learners aged 10–12 at CEFR A2 moving to B1. Every lesson is built
on one of ten Jurassic English stories. Learners read the story in their printed Storybook Workbook, quote it with
chapter numbers, and learn to defend a view with evidence.


The method
Each four-lesson unit follows one story through the Jurassic Thinking Cycle. Excavation (Analyze) looks closely
for evidence. Mapping the Divergence (Evaluate) weighs two defensible readings of a Big Question. The
Justification (Justify) builds a CEIW paragraph: Claim, Evidence, Interpretation, Warrant. The Impact
(Reflect) links the story to people, places and the living world. Unit 1 opens with a Justification lesson that needs
no reading, so the year starts with a paragraph every learner can attempt.


How a lesson runs
Lessons run 45–60 minutes. Each plan gives the target level, goals and objectives, the materials, a timed lesson
grid, the regulation routine, Accountable Talk prompts, differentiation tiers, a rubric and a closing routine. Term
milestones build across the year: blank-paper writing from Lesson 11, student-led seminars from Lesson 14, a
portfolio milestone at Lesson 27, an integrated synthesis from Lesson 28, and the capstone in Lessons 39 and 40.


The ten units
     Unit              Lessons          Story

       1                 1–4            The Song They Took Out

       2                 5–8            The Last Seat on the Night Ferry

       3                9–12            The Unsent Weather Report

       4                13–16           The Captain of the Old Van

       5                17–20           The Honest Scale

       6                21–24           Mai and the Season of Seeds

       7               25–28            The Voice in Maya’s Tablet

       8                29–32           Kit and the Invisible Line

       9                33–36           Leo and the Paper Theatre

      10                37–40           The Last Clue on Lantern Street


Seven of the ten stories are new Jurassic English originals; the other three (The Last Seat on the Night Ferry, The
Unsent Weather Report and The Voice in Maya’s Tablet) are existing Jurassic English stories. All ten have their
own Storybook Workbook and Teacher Book. The Student Workbook has one page for each of the 40 lessons.

Jurassic English · Level 3 Teacher Pack


     Lesson 1: The Justification — Constructing the Independent
    Justify

CEIW Paragraph (text-independent opener)

Target Grade Level / Subject / Duration
Grade Level: Ages 10–12 (CEFR A2 → B1)
Subject: English Language Arts (Jurassic English™ Level 3: Expansion)
Duration: 45–60 minutes
Core text: The Song They Took Out (Jurassic English original storybook workbook, Level 3). Thinking Cycle
stage: Justification.


Overall Learning Goals
Students begin Level 3 by writing a complete, unscaffolded CEIW paragraph (Claim, Evidence, Interpretation,
Warrant) on a dilemma that needs no prior reading. The dilemma previews the year’s first JE story, The Song
They Took Out, without spoiling it. The lesson sets the standard for the year: an opinion is not accepted without
evidence, and the warrant (the “So what?”) is the core reasoning move.


Specific Learning Objectives
 1. Students will regulate using the Butterfly Hug, bilateral tapping or the Cool Down Pass before writing.
2. Students will state a clear, defensible claim on the opener dilemma.
3. Students will support the claim with one piece of evidence (a fact, an example or a short quotation from the
   chapter 1 extract) and interpret it in their own words.
4. Students will write a warrant that answers “So what?” and survives a partner’s question.


Materials Needed
Core Text: The Song They Took Out, one printed Jurassic English storybook workbook per learner. Learners
quote the story with chapter numbers.
Accountable Talk Reference Cards (Marking, Pressing, Extending).

B1 Interpretive Marker Poster: “The author implies… / This evidence suggests… / The underlying assumption
is…”.

Coloured Index Cards (Yellow = Claim, Blue = Evidence, Green = Interpretation, Pink = Warrant) for the
Executive Dysfunction tier.

Visible Pomodoro timer; Cool Down Passes at the front desk; the Regulation Station.
Opener dilemma card: “A town removes every sad song, story and photograph so that nobody is ever unhappy. Is
this a good idea?”
Chapter 1 of The Song They Took Out on the board as the only text extract (“The tidiest town”).
Student Workbook page: Lesson 1, The independent CEIW paragraph.


Detailed Procedure / Step-by-Step Outline

Phase 1: Regulation & Metacognitive Preparation (0–5 minutes)
Activity: self-initiated regulation; orientation to the year.

Teacher Scripting Prompt: “Welcome to Level 3, Paleontologists. This year we stop asking only what happened.
We ask what it means and why it matters. Settle your body first: Butterfly Hug, tapping or a Cool Down Pass.”

Phase 2: The Dilemma (5–15 minutes)
Activity: reading the chapter 1 extract and the dilemma card.

Teacher Scripting Prompt: “Listen to the opening of our first story: “In Fairhollow, nobody ever cried at the
cinema, because there was nothing sad to see.” (chapter 1) Now the dilemma: is a town with nothing sad in it a
good idea? Decide, but do not tell anyone yet.”
Student Task: write a one-sentence claim on a sticky note.

Phase 3: The CEIW Sprint (15–35 minutes)
Activity: independent CEIW drafting with the Pomodoro Drafting Protocol (10 minutes writing, 3-minute
physical reset, 5-minute revision).
Teacher Scripting Prompt: “Claim. Evidence: a fact, an example from life, or a short quotation from chapter 1.
Interpretation: what that evidence means, in your words, using suggests that. Warrant: why the evidence proves
your claim. Pen down at the buzzer.”

Teacher Move: mark for architecture, not for opinion. “Your warrant connects to your claim. I cannot tell which
side I agree with, and that is how it should be.”

Phase 4: The “So What?” Drill (35–43 minutes)
Activity: partner pressure-test.
Teacher Scripting Prompt: “Your partner reads your paragraph back and asks: So what? Keep answering until
you reach a principle. “Because people would be happy” is not a warrant yet. What does happiness need?”
Student Task: revise the warrant once in a different colour.


Differentiation / Accommodations
Neuroinclusive (ADHD / Executive Dysfunction): Index Card Architecture. The learner lays out the C, E, I and W
cards on the desk before writing or speaking. Movement breaks between phases.

Neuroinclusive (Anxiety / ASD): share the lesson structure 10 minutes in advance. No cold calling. A learner may
give a spoken turn to the teacher privately, or pass.

Neuroinclusive (Dyslexia): the chapter is read aloud by the teacher or a partner; the learner may dictate or record
answers. Spelling is not marked today, only reasoning.
Support Tier: A paragraph frame with the four labels; the evidence is chosen with the teacher.

Core Tier: Blank CEIW boxes in the Student Workbook; independent.
Extension Tier: Write a counter-claim sentence and answer it inside the warrant.


Assessment & Rubric
Assessment Type: Diagnostic — First Independent CEIW of the Year

    Specific Learning
                         Emerging (A2)           Developing (A2+)                      Proficient (B1)                        Mastery (B1+)

Jurassic English · Teacher Book · Level 3                                                                                             The Song They Took Out


How to teach this book
Thinking Cycle, quick path, two-week unit plan, chant and phonics

The Jurassic Thinking Cycle has four steps. In this book each step is tied to one chapter. Learners meet it on
student page 18.

 Step                  Chapter        What learners do

   Analyze             4              Excavation · In chapter 4, which clue explains why the herons left the river?
                                      Answer: B. When the reeds were cut, the fish had nowhere to hide.
                                      Clue: When the reeds were cut, the fish had nowhere to hide.

   Evaluate            5              Divergence Map · Was the Calm Office protecting people, or taking something from them?
                                      Build a case for each view before you choose.
                                      Choices: Protecting people / Both / Taking something away. Any view supported by a story
                                      clue.

   Justify             5              Justification · Write a claim, evidence from the text, an interpretation in your own words and a
                                      warrant (why the evidence supports the claim).
                                      Word bank: protect, missing, choose, verse, herons, truth

   Reflect             6              Impact · The reeds were cut to make the river tidy, and the herons left. Name a place near
                                      you that is tidy but may not be healthy for living things. What one change could help?
                                      Answers vary: open to the learner’s own experience.


Quick path: three sessions

  Session 1 · Excavation: what was taken out · 40 min
   1. Read chapters 1–2 aloud. Pause at “She did not know yet what neat could cost” and ask what the words
      suggest, not only what they say.
   2. Do each chapter’s Read and circle and Think about it questions; for every answer, learners quote the words
      that support it.
   3. Discuss: why might a town want to remove every sad thing? List what it gains and what it loses.
   4. Model: “The phrase __ suggests __ because __.”



  Session 2 · Mapping the Divergence: protection or loss? · 40 min
   1. Read chapters 3–5 aloud.
   2. Chart two columns: what the Calm Office protects people from, and what it takes away. Add a chapter
      number to every row.
   3. Ask: why does the happy verse sound different after the sad one? What does that suggest about feelings?
   4. Put the six chapters in order and summarise each in one sentence.
